title: Breathing player with nose and mouth counts
what: Nested circles with the word Exhale in the middle and a small pill above showing breathe in through the nose for 4 and out through the mouth for 6.
takeaway: Show the pattern as two tiny icons with counts so an older user knows nose or mouth and how long, without reading a paragraph.

title: Breathing orb with phase markers
what: A soft glowing orb with a thin ring and dots marking each phase, the words Breathe In below, and like, pause and sound buttons.
takeaway: Markers on a ring let the user see where they are in the cycle, and a single big pause button is easy to hit.

title: Simple inhale circle with progress bar
what: Flat purple screen with nested circles reading Inhale and Nose, a thin progress bar and a full width Pause button.
takeaway: A plain flat shape plus a session progress bar is enough; no video or texture is needed for the player to work.

title: Breathing techniques as tiles
what: A grid of dark tiles for Physiological Sigh, Box, 4-7-8 and Coherent Breathing, each with its own dot pattern and a bookmark.
takeaway: Give each technique its own small visual so users can pick by shape and remember their favourite, which suits a fixed set like box, 4-7-8 and cyclic sigh.

title: Technique picker with purpose tags
what: A box outline above a list of techniques, each tagged Rest, Balance or Energy, with a tick on the chosen one and a Save button.
takeaway: A one word purpose tag next to each pattern helps people choose by need (calm down, wake up) instead of by name.

title: Technique list with use case and minutes
what: Cards for Box Breathing, 4-7-8, Cyclic Sighing, Diaphragmatic and Physiological Sigh, each with a one line benefit, a coloured use case chip and a duration.
takeaway: Showing minutes on every card tells a busy user up front that a session is only 1 to 5 minutes.

title: Choose method and duration before starting
what: A setup card for Box breathing with a short description, two method cards (4-7-8 and Box), a 10 min duration ruler and a Start button.
takeaway: Pattern and length can sit on one setup screen with a sensible default, so starting is a single tap.

title: Completion with breath count and streak
what: A large 60 Breaths number inside a woven ring, a level up line, streak and total sessions tiles and a Continue button.
takeaway: A single big number for what was done is a clear win moment; GoodFlip can keep the number and skip levels.

title: Breathing complete with why it helps
what: A cloud illustration, the title Breathing Complete, one sentence on how breathing lowers stress, a thumbs up or down row and Return to Home.
takeaway: One short line on why it helped plus a quick thumbs rating closes the session gently and collects feedback.

title: Evening mood face slider
what: A question addressing the user by name about this evening, a big smiling face with the word Good, and a five face slider underneath.
takeaway: A morning or evening greeting plus one big face that changes with the slider makes the twice daily check-in feel personal and quick.

title: Morning mood grid with emoji words
what: Good morning greeting over a three by four grid of emoji plus word buttons such as Happy, Grateful, Tired, Anxious and Sad.
takeaway: Pairing an emoji with a word in big tappable tiles makes one tap logging possible for users who will not move a slider.

title: State of Mind: what best describes this feeling
what: After choosing Very Pleasant, a glowing flower sits above chips of feeling words like Hopeful, Grateful and Calm, with Show More and Next.
takeaway: Only show words that match the chosen level, which keeps the list short and easy to scan.

title: What is causing this feeling
what: A grid of icon tiles such as Community, Family, Friends, Health and Hobbies, with three selected, and an Add to journal button.
takeaway: A context step with icons for family, friends and health could double as the social connection signal for the Mind score.

title: State of Mind month calendar
what: A month grid where logged days show a coloured flower and empty days show an outline circle, with today marked.
takeaway: Empty outlines for missed days and a colour per logged day make the month readable at a glance without any numbers.

title: Mood calendar, one dot per day
what: A tall grid of dots labelled by month, with logged days filled blue or pink and sized differently, under the line One dot = One day.
takeaway: A dot field shows months of history in one screen and stays calm even when most days are empty.

title: What you were doing and how you felt
what: An analysis screen with stacked coloured discs above activities like Working, Doing Art, Hanging Out and Eating, and a next section for who you were with.
takeaway: Linking activities and company to mood is the insight that makes logging a pleasant activity worth doing.

title: Activity picker with custom add
what: Round icon buttons for activities such as Music, Good Meal, Time Alone, Helping Others and Health, each with an edit menu, plus an add button.
takeaway: A grid of everyday activities with simple glyphs is a ready model for the one pleasant activity a day log, with room to add local ones.

title: Daily prompt card: Say Hi To Someone
what: A dated card for today titled Say Hi To Someone, with a short paragraph suggesting greeting a neighbour or colleague and a Write button.
takeaway: One concrete social action per day, written warmly, is a simple shape for the meaningful connection prompt.

title: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
flow: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
what: A sheet for the alternate breathing exercise with a one line description, a 1, 2 or 4 min choice and Begin Breathing.
takeaway: Offer only three durations as plain text options so choosing takes one tap.

title: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
flow: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
what: A 3 count ring with the words Get comfortable and a hint to sit or lie down.
takeaway: A short get ready countdown gives the user time to settle before the first breath.

title: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
flow: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
what: A grey circle with the count 1, the instruction Inhale Right nostril, a timer reading 00:20 of 01:14 and a Finish Earlier button.
takeaway: Show time done out of total and let people finish early without feeling they failed.

title: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
flow: Choosing and doing a breathing exercise
what: Good job title with breaths and time tiles, a Breathe Again button and a No, A little, Yes question about enjoyment.
takeaway: A three option enjoyment question is lighter than stars and could feed the Pleasure and Mood signal.

title: Logging a feeling from Home
what: A sheet asking How are you today with five soft faces from Awful to Great above an empty weekly mood chart.
takeaway: Start the check-in with one row of five faces; everything else is optional.

title: Logging a feeling from Home
what: After choosing Good, three feeling words are selected in green and a second group asks what is having the biggest impact.
takeaway: Words and context can live on one scrolling sheet so the flow does not feel like many steps.

title: Logging a feeling from Home
what: A confirmation headed I'm feeling good with the chosen face highlighted and a suggested gratitude meditation under For your mood.
takeaway: Right after a check-in, suggest one matching activity, such as a breathing session when stressed.

title: Logging a feeling from Home
what: The weekly Mood Analysis chart now shows a single green face on Monday.
takeaway: The first log appears in the trend immediately, so the user sees their entry counted.

title: Mood check-in with what you were doing
flow: Mood check-in with what you were doing
what: A home screen asking How are you feeling this evening with a partial yellow ring around a Check in button and day streak tiles.
takeaway: Name the time of day in the prompt so morning and evening check-ins feel like two separate small moments.

title: Mood check-in with what you were doing
flow: Mood check-in with what you were doing
what: Four coloured blobs split feelings into high or low energy and pleasant or unpleasant.
takeaway: A two axis first choice is quick, but older users may find energy versus pleasantness harder than plain faces.

title: Mood check-in with what you were doing
flow: Mood check-in with what you were doing
what: A field of yellow circles with feeling words, Proud selected, and a definition of the word in the bottom bar.
takeaway: Showing a short definition when a word is tapped helps people who are unsure what a word means.

title: Mood check-in with what you were doing
flow: Mood check-in with what you were doing
what: Chip groups for What are you doing, Who are you with and Where are you, with Crafting, Pets, Family and Home selected.
takeaway: Three short chip rows capture the pleasant activity and the social connection in the same check-in, no extra screen needed.

title: Mood check-in with what you were doing
flow: Mood check-in with what you were doing
what: The next morning prompt shows a full ring blended from green and yellow, one colour segment per past check-in.
takeaway: The home ring fills with each check-in's colour, a quiet record of the day that rewards logging without numbers.
